title: Acute appendicitis
text:
Luminal obstruction by a faecolith or lymphoid hyperplasia causes distension, bacterial overgrowth and mural ischaemia. Pain starts periumbilically (visceral afferents to T10 via the midgut) and shifts to McBurney's point once the parietal peritoneum is inflamed (somatic innervation).
The variable position of the appendix changes the picture: retrocaecal appendicitis irritates psoas (psoas sign), pelvic appendicitis irritates obturator internus (obturator sign) and can mimic urinary or gynaecological disease. The appendicular artery is an end artery, so gangrene and perforation follow quickly.
Most common tumour: appendiceal neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumour, usually found incidentally.

title: Gallstone disease
text:
Stones impacted in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct cause biliary colic and acute cholecystitis, with Murphy sign and pain referred to the right shoulder tip (phrenic nerve, C3-C5).
Choledocholithiasis leads to obstructive jaundice and ascending cholangitis (Charcot triad: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain). A stone at the ampulla can cause gallstone pancreatitis. A large stone eroding into the duodenum can obstruct the terminal ileum (gallstone ileus).
Mirizzi syndrome: a stone in the neck compresses the common hepatic duct. Painless enlargement with jaundice (Courvoisier sign) suggests pancreatic head malignancy instead.

title: Pancreatitis and pancreatic carcinoma
text:
Acute pancreatitis (gallstones, alcohol, hypertriglyceridaemia, ERCP) releases activated enzymes causing fat necrosis, haemorrhage (Grey Turner flank and Cullen periumbilical bruising), hypocalcaemia from saponification, ARDS and pseudocyst formation.
Adenocarcinoma of the head obstructs the common bile duct (painless jaundice, palpable gallbladder) and may invade the superior mesenteric vessels behind the neck, determining resectability. Body and tail tumours present late with back pain from coeliac plexus invasion. Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign) can herald it.

title: Peptic ulcer complications
text:
Posterior duodenal ulcers erode the gastroduodenal artery (major haemorrhage); anterior ulcers perforate, releasing air under the diaphragm. Gastric ulcers on the lesser curvature can erode the left gastric artery; a posterior gastric ulcer can erode the splenic artery or penetrate the pancreas.
Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) causes multiple, distal or refractory ulcers.

title: Hiatus hernia and gastric carcinoma
text:
Sliding hiatus hernias displace the gastro-oesophageal junction into the thorax and promote reflux; para-oesophageal (rolling) hernias keep the junction in place but can strangulate or volvulate.
Gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type linked to H. pylori and atrophic gastritis; diffuse 'signet-ring' type causing linitis plastica) may metastasise to the left supraclavicular node (Virchow node), periumbilical skin (Sister Mary Joseph nodule) and ovaries (Krukenberg tumour).

title: Oesophageal varices and Barrett oesophagus
text:
The lower oesophagus is a portosystemic anastomosis between left gastric (portal) and oesophageal (azygos) veins. In portal hypertension, submucosal varices form and can rupture with massive haematemesis.
Chronic reflux converts the distal squamous epithelium to intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells (Barrett metaplasia), the precursor of adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma (smoking, alcohol) favours the middle third.
The three physiological constrictions (cricopharyngeus, aortic arch/left main bronchus, diaphragmatic hiatus) are where foreign bodies lodge and caustic injuries are worst. Boerhaave syndrome is full-thickness rupture after forceful vomiting, usually of the left posterolateral distal wall.

title: Cirrhosis and portal hypertension
text:
Chronic injury (alcohol, hepatitis B/C, fatty liver disease) causes bridging fibrosis and regenerative nodules. Distorted sinusoids raise portal pressure, opening portosystemic anastomoses (oesophageal varices, caput medusae, rectal varices), causing splenomegaly with hypersplenism and ascites.
Loss of synthetic function lowers albumin and clotting factors; failure to clear ammonia causes hepatic encephalopathy; failure to metabolise oestrogen causes spider naevi, palmar erythema and gynaecomastia. Cirrhosis is the main precursor of hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Liver segments and resection
text:
The Couinaud system divides the liver into eight functionally independent segments, each with its own portal triad branch and hepatic venous drainage, allowing segmental resection. Cantlie's line (gallbladder fossa to IVC) separates the functional right and left lobes, not the falciform ligament.
The Pringle manoeuvre (clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament through the epiploic foramen) controls inflow bleeding during hepatic trauma or surgery.

title: Splenic rupture and asplenia
text:
The most commonly injured abdominal organ in blunt trauma, especially with fractures of left ribs 9 to 11 or in infectious mononucleosis (splenomegaly makes it vulnerable, so contact sports are avoided). Pain may be referred to the left shoulder (Kehr sign).
After splenectomy, patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection by encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus) and need vaccination. Blood films show Howell-Jolly bodies.
Accessory spleens (splenunculi) near the hilum can cause relapse of ITP after splenectomy.

title: Duodenal atresia and superior mesenteric artery syndrome
text:
Duodenal atresia (failed recanalisation, strongly associated with Down syndrome) causes bilious vomiting in neonates and a 'double bubble' on X-ray. Annular pancreas, from abnormal rotation of the ventral bud, can encircle and obstruct the second part.
The third part crosses between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery; rapid weight loss reduces the aortomesenteric angle and compresses it (SMA syndrome), causing postprandial vomiting.

title: Meckel diverticulum and Crohn disease
text:
Meckel diverticulum, a remnant of the vitello-intestinal duct on the antimesenteric border of the ileum ('rule of 2s': 2% of people, about 2 feet from the ileocaecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue). Ectopic gastric mucosa secretes acid, causing painless rectal bleeding in children; it can also cause intussusception, volvulus or diverticulitis mimicking appendicitis.
Crohn disease classically affects the terminal ileum with transmural inflammation, skip lesions, strictures, fistulae and malabsorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts (gallstones, oxalate kidney stones).

title: Diverticular disease and sigmoid volvulus
text:
High intraluminal pressure pushes mucosa through weak points where the vasa recta penetrate the wall, forming false (pulsion) diverticula, most often in the sigmoid. Complications include diverticulitis ('left-sided appendicitis'), abscess, perforation, colovesical fistula (pneumaturia) and painless haemorrhage.
The long mobile sigmoid mesocolon allows volvulus in elderly and institutionalised patients, producing a 'coffee bean' sign on X-ray.

title: Colorectal carcinoma by site
text:
Right-sided tumours (wide lumen, liquid stool) present with iron-deficiency anaemia and weight loss; left-sided tumours present with change in bowel habit, obstruction and fresh bleeding. Most arise from adenomatous polyps; the adenoma-carcinoma sequence involves APC, KRAS and TP53 mutations, while Lynch syndrome tumours favour the right colon.
Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteraemia or endocarditis should prompt colonoscopy. Metastasis follows the portal vein to the liver.
In ulcerative colitis, toxic megacolon most often dilates the transverse colon.

title: Rectal carcinoma and haemorrhoids
text:
Rectal cancers spread to mesorectal nodes, so total mesorectal excision within the mesorectal fascia is standard. Low tumours near the anal verge may require abdominoperineal resection.
Internal haemorrhoids are cushions of the superior rectal venous plexus above the pectinate line: painless bleeding, visceral innervation. External haemorrhoids below the line are somatically innervated (pudendal) and very painful when thrombosed. The pectinate line also divides lymph drainage (internal iliac vs superficial inguinal nodes) and cancer type (adenocarcinoma vs squamous cell).

title: Renal calculi and pyelonephritis
text:
Stones lodge at the three ureteric narrowings: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim over the iliac vessels and the vesicoureteric junction. Ureteric colic radiates from loin to groin (T11-L2 visceral afferents). Most stones are calcium oxalate; struvite staghorn calculi form in infection with urease-producing Proteus; uric acid stones are radiolucent.
Ascending infection (vesicoureteric reflux, obstruction, pregnancy) causes pyelonephritis with loin pain, fever and white cell casts; chronic reflux scars the upper and lower poles, where compound papillae permit intrarenal reflux.

title: Renal cell carcinoma and congenital anomalies
text:
Clear-cell RCC arises from proximal tubular epithelium (VHL loss); classic triad of haematuria, flank pain and a mass. It can grow into the renal vein and IVC, cause a left varicocele (left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein) and produce polycythaemia (erythropoietin) or hypercalcaemia (PTHrP).
Horseshoe kidney: fused lower poles are trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery, prone to obstruction, stones and associated with Turner syndrome. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease causes massive bilateral cysts, hypertension and berry aneurysms.

title: Bladder rupture and urothelial carcinoma
text:
A full bladder rises above the pubic symphysis: a blow to the lower abdomen can rupture its dome intraperitoneally (urinary ascites), while pelvic fractures cause extraperitoneal rupture near the neck.
Urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma causes painless haematuria and is linked to smoking, aromatic amines (dye and rubber industry) and cyclophosphamide. Schistosoma haematobium infection causes squamous cell carcinoma. The trigone is embryologically mesodermal, derived from the mesonephric ducts.

title: Benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer
text:
BPH arises in the transition zone around the prostatic urethra, causing obstructive urinary symptoms, urinary retention, bladder trabeculation and hydronephrosis; it is driven by dihydrotestosterone (hence 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors).
Adenocarcinoma usually arises in the peripheral zone, the part felt on digital rectal examination, so it causes symptoms late. It metastasises to vertebrae via the valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus), producing osteoblastic lesions and back pain.

title: Testicular torsion and germ cell tumours
text:
A high investment of the tunica vaginalis (bell-clapper deformity) lets the testis rotate on its spermatic cord, occluding venous then arterial flow. Sudden severe pain in adolescents, a high-riding horizontal testis and loss of the cremasteric reflex demand surgery within about 6 hours to save the testis; the other side is fixed too.
Germ cell tumours (seminoma, embryonal, yolk sac, choriocarcinoma, teratoma) spread by lymphatics to para-aortic nodes at the renal hila, following the testicular vessels' embryological descent, not to inguinal nodes. Scrotal violation during biopsy is avoided for this reason. Cryptorchidism raises the risk.

title: Varicocele
text:
Dilatation of the pampiniform plexus ('bag of worms'), far more common on the left because the left testicular vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle, is longer and can be compressed between the aorta and SMA (nutcracker phenomenon). It is associated with reduced fertility due to raised testicular temperature.
A new right-sided or a non-reducing varicocele (lying down) should raise suspicion of a retroperitoneal mass or renal tumour obstructing venous return.

title: Penile fracture, priapism and Peyronie disease
text:
Penile fracture: rupture of the tunica albuginea of an erect corpus cavernosum during intercourse, with a crack, detumescence and 'aubergine' swelling; urethral injury through the corpus spongiosum must be excluded.
Ischaemic priapism (sickle cell disease, intracavernosal drugs, trazodone) is a compartment syndrome of the corpora cavernosa causing fibrosis and erectile dysfunction if not decompressed within hours. The corpus spongiosum and glans are spared, which remain soft.
Peyronie disease: fibrous plaques in the tunica albuginea cause painful curvature.

title: Vasectomy, epididymitis and congenital absence
text:
The ductus deferens is palpable as a firm cord in the spermatic cord and is divided in vasectomy through the scrotal skin; sperm persist in the distal tract for weeks.
Epididymitis (Chlamydia/gonorrhoea in young men, E. coli in older men with outflow obstruction) causes gradual pain relieved by elevation (Prehn sign), unlike torsion.
Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens is associated with CFTR mutations and causes obstructive azoospermia.

title: Bile duct injury and cholangiocarcinoma
text:
The commonest serious complication of cholecystectomy is mistaking the common bile duct for the cystic duct; safe dissection of Calot's triangle (cystic duct, common hepatic duct, liver edge containing the cystic artery) is designed to prevent it.
Cholangiocarcinoma at the hilar confluence (Klatskin tumour) causes painless jaundice, and is linked to primary sclerosing cholangitis (with ulcerative colitis) and liver flukes. Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations that also carry malignant risk.
